headline: In rengō, 連 is a daiyōji replacing 聯.
Kari was the stem of classical 借る (karu, “to borrow”), and is now also the stem of 借りる (kariru).
Todana is 戸 (to, “door”) plus 棚 (tana, “shelf”), with tana voiced to dana.
Shomotsu is first attested in the 1920s.
Inochi is probably 息 (i, “breath”) plus の (no) plus 霊 (chi, “spirit, force, soul”).
Nuno is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *nono.
Kion appeared in the Seimi Kaisō of 1837-1847.
Kara, “empty”, is cognate with 殻 (kara, “shell”).
Soshiki is Middle Chinese 組織, “to weave threads together; to form from smaller components”.
Tsubu is not attested until a Muromachi-period text, and an earlier form tsubi may have preceded it.
Teki is from Middle Chinese 敵 (MC dek), first cited in Japanese in the early 1200s.
Arukōru began as arukohoru, borrowed from Dutch alcohol with a phonetic kanji spelling.
Sōzoku is Middle Chinese 相續, literally “successively, one after another + to succeed, to continue”, first attested in Japanese in 820.
Shikata ga nai is literally “there is no way”.
Shokyū began as shokipu, from the Middle Chinese compound 初級, literally “beginning + level, grade”.
Miageru is 見る (miru, “to see, look”) plus 上げる (ageru, “to raise”).
Bunseki is Literary Chinese 分析 (fēnxī, “to separate, divide or split apart”).
Hōkō is from Middle Chinese 方向 (MC pjang xjangH).
Okawari is 御 (o-) plus 代わり (kawari, “compensation”).
Kumu, “to draw”, is likely the same word as 斟む (kumu, “to consider people's feelings”) and 酌む (kumu, “to serve sake”).
Ureru is the potential form of 売る (uru, “to sell”).
Yowameru is 弱 (yowa, root of 弱い, “weak”) plus -meru, “-en, -ify”.
Arai, “coarse”, is cognate with 荒い (arai).
Mijikai was mizikasi in Old Japanese, first attested in c. 759 in the Man'yōshū; its constituent parts remain obscure.
Gekijō is 劇 (geki, “drama”) plus 場 (jō, “place”).
In kesseki, 欠 is a daiyōji replacing 缺.
Saikō is 最 (sai-, “most”) plus 高 (kō, “high”).
Hisashiburi is 久しい (hisashii, “long”) plus 振り (-buri, “first time after”).
Tojiru is from Old Japanese 閉づ (tozu), and the distinction between ぢ and じ was lost over time.
Ura, “back”, is simply from Old Japanese.
Kiiro is 黄 (ki, “yellow”) plus 色 (iro, “colour”).
